parts.article:
Inside the mind of a fan
 
How watching sport affects the brain
 
A At about the same time that the poet Homer invented the epic there, the ancient Greeks started a festival in which men competed in a single race, about 200 metres long. The winner received a branch of wild olives. The Greeks called this celebration the Olympics. Though the ancient sprint remains, today the Olympics are far more than that. Indeed, the Games seem to celebrate the dream of progress as embodied in the human form. That the Games are intoxicating to watch is beyond question. During the Athens Olympics in 2004, 3.4 billion people, half the world, watched them on television. Certainly, being a spectator is a thrilling experience—but why?
 
B In 1996, three Italian neuroscientists, Giacomo Rizzolatti, Leonardo Fogassi and Vittorio Gallese, examined the premotor cortex of monkeys. They discovered that inside these primate brains there were groups of cells that 'store vocabularies of motor actions', just as there are grammars of movement. These networks of cells are the bodily 'sentences' we use every day, the ones our brain has chosen to retain and refine. Think, for example, about a golf swing. To those who have only watched the Masters Tournament on TV, golfing seems easy. To the novice, however, the skill of casting a smooth arc with a lopsided metal stick is virtually impossible. This is because most novices swing with their consciousness, using an area of the brain next to the premotor cortex. To the expert, on the other hand, a perfectly balanced stroke is second nature. For him, the motor action has become memorized, and the movements are embedded in the neurons of his premotor cortex. He hits the ball with the tranquility of his perfected autopilot.
 
C These neurons in the premotor cortex, besides explaining why certain athletes seem to possess almost unbelievable levels of skill, have an even more amazing characteristic, one that caused Rizzolatti, Fogassi and Gallese to give them the lofty title 'mirror neurons'. They note that 'the main functional characteristic of mirror neurons is that they become active both when the monkey performs a particular action (for example, grasping an object or holding it) and, astonishingly, when it sees another individual performing a similar action'. Humans have an even more elaborate mirror neuron system. These peculiar cells mirror, inside the brain, the outside world: they enable us to internalize the actions of another. In order to be activated, though, these cells require what the scientists call 'goal-orientated movements'. If we are staring at a photograph, a fixed image of a runner mid-stride, our mirror neurons are totally silent. They only fire when the runner is active: running, moving or sprinting.
 
D What these electrophysiological studies indicate is that when we watch a golfer or a runner in action, the mirror neurons in our own premotor cortex light up as if we were the ones competing. This phenomenon of neural mirroring was first discovered in 1954, when two French physiologists, Gastaut and Bert, found that the brains of humans vibrate with two distinct wavelengths, alpha and mu. The mu system is involved in neural mirroring. It is active when our bodies are still, and disappears whenever we do something active, like playing a sport or changing the TV channel. The surprising fact is that the mu signal is also quiet when we watch someone else being active, as on TV. These results are the effect of mirror neurons.
 
E Rizzolatti, Fogassi and Gallese call the idea of mirror neurons the 'direct matching hypothesis'. They believe that we only understand the movement of sports stars when we 'map the visual representation of the observed action onto our motor representation of the same action'. According to this theory, watching an Olympic athlete 'causes the motor system of the observer to resonate. The 'motor knowledge' of the observer is used to understand the observed action.' But mirror neurons are more than just the neural basis for our attitude to sport. It turns out that watching a great golfer makes us better golfers, and watching a great sprinter actually makes us run faster. This ability to learn by watching is a crucial skill. From the acquisition of language as infants to learning facial expressions, mimesis (copying) is an essential part of being conscious. The best athletes are those with a premotor cortex capable of imagining the movements of victory, together with the physical properties to make those movements real.
 
F But how many of us regularly watch sports in order to be a better athlete? Rather, we watch sport for the feeling, the human drama. This feeling also derives from mirror neurons. By letting spectators share in the motions of victory, they also allow us to share in its feelings. This is because they are directly connected to the amygdala, one of the main brain regions involved in emotion. During the Olympics, the mirror neurons of whole nations will be electrically identical, their athletes causing spectators to feel, just for a second or two, the same thing. Watching sports brings people together. Most of us will never run a mile in under four minutes, or hit a home run. Our consolation comes in watching. When we gather around the TV, we all feel, just for a moment, what it is to do something perfectly.

questions.question: an explanation of why watching sport may be emotionally satisfying

analyses.content: “Emotionally satisfying” 对应 “share in its feelings / connected to the amygdala / consolation”。
(Paragraph F) “Rather, we watch sport for the feeling... they also allow us to share in its feelings.”
题目提到解释为什么看体育比赛会在情感上令人满足。原文F段提到我们看体育是为了“feeling（感觉）”和“human drama（人性的戏剧）”，镜像神经元让我们“share in its feelings（分享感觉）”，并连接到处理情绪的“amygdala（杏仁核）”，这解释了情感满足的原因。

questions.question: an explanation of why beginners find sporting tasks difficult

analyses.content: 题目提到解释为什么初学者觉得体育任务很难。原文B段对比了新手和专家，指出新手“swing with their consciousness（用意识挥杆）”，使用前运动皮层旁边的区域，导致“virtually impossible（几乎不可能/很难）”。
“Beginners find... difficult” 对应 “To the novice... virtually impossible”。
(Paragraph B) “To the novice, however, the skill... is virtually impossible. This is because most novices swing with their consciousness...”

questions.question: a factor that needs to combine with mirroring to attain sporting excellence

analyses.content: 题目提到一个需要与镜像结合以达到体育卓越的因素。原文E段末尾提到最好的运动员拥有能想象胜利动作的前运动皮层，但这必须“together with the physical properties（连同身体素质/属性）”才能让动作成真。
“Factor... combine with” 对应 “together with the physical properties”。
(Paragraph E) “The best athletes are those with a premotor cortex... together with the physical properties to make those movements real.”

questions.question: a comparison of human and animal mirror neurons

analyses.content: (Paragraph C) “Humans have an even more elaborate mirror neuron system.”
题目提到人类和动物镜像神经元的比较。原文C段在介绍完猴子的发现后，紧接着说“Humans have an even more elaborate mirror neuron system（人类拥有更精细的镜像神经元系统）”，进行了直接比较。
“Comparison” 对应 “Humans have an even more elaborate...”。

questions.question: the first discovery of brain activity related to mirror neurons

analyses.content: 题目提到关于镜像神经元相关大脑活动的首次发现。原文D段提到神经镜像现象“was first discovered in 1954（于1954年首次被发现）”，由Gastaut和Bert发现。
“First discovery” 对应 “first discovered in 1954”。
(Paragraph D) “This phenomenon of neural mirroring was first discovered in 1954...”

questions.question: a claim linking observation to improvement in performance

analyses.content: 题目提到将观察与表现提升联系起来的主张。原文E段提到“watching a great golfer makes us better golfers（看伟大的高尔夫球手让我们成为更好的球手）”，即观察能提升表现。
“Linking observation to improvement” 对应 “watching... makes us better / run faster”。
(Paragraph E) “It turns out that watching a great golfer makes us better golfers...”

options.option: a system of words about movement
options.optionContent: a system of words about movement

questions.question: The writer uses the term 'grammar of movement' to mean

analyses.content: 题目问“运动的语法（grammar of movement）”是指什么？原文B段说细胞群存储运动动作的词汇，“just as there are grammars of movement. These networks of cells are the bodily 'sentences'...（就像有运动的语法一样。这些细胞网络是身体的'句子'……）”。这里是用语法来比喻**细胞网络（network of cells）**的结构化功能，对应选项 C (a pattern of connected cells)。
这是一个比喻（metaphor），不要选B（真的单词系统）；它指代的是前面的 “groups of cells” 和后面的 “networks of cells”。
(Paragraph B) “...groups of cells that 'store vocabularies of motor actions', just as there are grammars of movement. These networks of cells...”

options.option: by planning each phase of movement
options.optionContent: by planning each phase of movement

options.option: by thinking about the actions of others
options.optionContent: by thinking about the actions of others

questions.question: The writer states that expert players perform their actions

analyses.content: “Without conscious thought” 对应 “second nature / autopilot”。
(Paragraph B) “To the expert... a perfectly balanced stroke is second nature... hits the ball with the tranquility of his perfected autopilot.”
题目问作者说专家级选手如何执行动作？原文B段提到对于专家，动作是“second nature（第二天性）”，“autopilot（自动驾驶）”，且对比新手（用consciousness），专家是“memorized（内化记忆）”的，意味着无需有意识思考，对应选项 A (without conscious thought)。

options.option: feel linked with people of different nationalities
options.optionContent: feel linked with people of different nationalities

questions.question: The writer states that the most common motive for watching sport is to

analyses.content: 题目问看体育比赛最常见的动机是什么？原文F段明确说：“we watch sport for the feeling（我们看体育是为了感觉）”，并提到这种感觉让我们体验“share in its feelings”，对应选项 C (experience strong positive emotions)。
虽然文中提到了 bringing people together (B)，但这更多是结果而非首要动机（motive）；A（提升表现）被文中 “how many of us...?” 的反问否定了。
(Paragraph F) “Rather, we watch sport for the feeling... allow us to share in its feelings.”

questions.question: Inexpert sports players are too aware of what they are doing.

analyses.content: 题目说不熟练的运动员（inexpert sports players）过分关注自己在做什么。原文B段说新手（novices）“swing with their consciousness（带着意识挥杆）”，这使得动作几乎不可能完成。Use consciousness 即“too aware”，题目与原文一致，选 YES。
“Inexpert” 对应 “novice”，“Too aware” 对应 “swing with their consciousness”。
(Paragraph B) “This is because most novices swing with their consciousness...”

questions.question: Monkeys have a more complex mirror neuron system than humans.

analyses.content: (Paragraph C) “Humans have an even more elaborate mirror neuron system.”
题目说猴子的镜像神经元系统比人类更复杂。原文C段明确说“Humans have an even more elaborate mirror neuron system（人类拥有更精细/复杂的镜像神经元系统）”，题目说反了，选 NO。
比较级方向反了。

questions.question: Looking at a photograph can activate mirror neurons.

analyses.content: 题目说看照片可以激活镜像神经元。原文C段说：“If we are staring at a photograph... our mirror neurons are totally silent（如果我们盯着照片看……我们的镜像神经元完全静默）”，题目与原文矛盾，选 NO。
“Activate” 与 “totally silent” 矛盾。
(Paragraph C) “If we are staring at a photograph... our mirror neurons are totally silent.”

questions.question: Gastaut and Bert were both researchers and sports players.

analyses.content: 题目说Gastaut和Bert既是研究人员又是运动员。原文D段只介绍他们是“two French physiologists（两位法国生理学家/研究人员）”，未提及他们是否是运动员，选 NOT GIVEN。
文中只提到了职业身份（physiologists），未提爱好或第二身份。
(Paragraph D) “...two French physiologists, Gastaut and Bert...”

questions.question: The mu system is at rest when we are engaged in an activity.

analyses.content: 题目说当我们从事活动时，mu系统处于静息状态（at rest/inactive）。原文D段说mu系统在身体静止时活跃（active），而在我们做活跃的事情时“disappears（消失/不活跃）”。这里的“at rest”指的是“不活跃/静默”的状态，与“disappears”一致，选 YES。
这里的 “at rest” 是指神经信号的“休息/不工作”状态，对应原文的 “disappears / quiet”。
(Paragraph D) “...disappears whenever we do something active...”
